drawing-exam-ready-graphs: What separates a graph that earns full marks from one that looks right but scores nothing?
unit-1-scarcity: Even the richest person on Earth cannot have everything. Why not?
What four kinds of resources go into making even a simple loaf of bread?
Why does each extra unit of one thing cost a country more and more of another?
Who decides what gets made: prices, planners or a mix of the two?
Why do countries buy from abroad things they could make perfectly well at home?
Water keeps us alive and diamonds do not, so why do diamonds cost so much more?
unit-2-demand: With no one in charge, how do millions of buyers and sellers end up producing what people want?
Why do economists insist that a price cut does not increase demand?
Why do farmers grow more when prices rise, and what makes them grow less at every price?
Why do some buyers barely react when a price jumps, while others switch away at once?
When a seller charges more, why does the money coming in sometimes go up and sometimes go down?
When prices jump, why can some producers flood the market while others cannot grow more for years?
When people get richer, why do they buy less of some things?
unit-2-equilibrium-surplus: When a price is too high or too low, what pulls it back to where buyers and sellers agree?
When a harvest fails or buyers rush in, which way do prices move, and how far?
When you would gladly pay more than the price, where does that extra value go?
If buyers and sellers both gain from a trade, how can a free market still produce the wrong amount?
unit-2-government-intervention-markets: What happens when a government makes something cheaper by law?
Why would a government ever make something cost more?
When a government taxes sugary drinks, who really pays the tax: the shoppers or the companies?
When a government pays firms for every item they make, who ends up with the money?
When a country taxes goods from abroad, who ends up paying, and who comes out ahead?
unit-3-long-run-production-costs: Why do some industries have thousands of small firms while others have only two or three?
Why can a giant firm make things more cheaply than a small one, and when does size start to hurt?
Why do some markets have thousands of sellers while others have only one or two?
Why might a business that brings in money every year still be making no real profit?
Why would a business stop making more when each extra sale still brings in money?
unit-3-long-run-production-costs-part-2: If a seller must cut its price to sell one more, why does that extra sale bring in less than the price?
Why can't one wheat farmer charge even slightly more than the market price?
Can a firm make goods at the lowest possible cost and still waste resources?
When a product is very profitable and anyone can start selling it, where do the profits go?
unit-3-production-function: If a kitchen hires twice as many cooks, why might it not make twice as many meals?
Why can the next batch of bread cost a bakery more to make than the batches before it?
How could ten workers make thousands of pins a day when one alone could barely make twenty?
unit-4-monopoly: If one company controls a whole market, why doesn't it just charge the highest price it can?
Why might it make sense for only one company to lay the water pipes in a city?
Why can two people sitting side by side on the same train have paid very different fares?
Why can a popular new kind of café make big profits at first, then only just cover its costs later?
When only a few big firms share a market, why do their prices so often move together?
How can two rival firms each make their best choice and still both end up worse off?
unit-5-introduction-factor-markets: Nobody buys workers for their own sake, so what decides how many a business wants to hire?
What makes people willing to do a job, and why isn't the pay the whole story?
Why do some of the most useful jobs pay less than jobs that seem far less useful?
Why would a firm refuse to hire a worker who would add more to its sales than they are paid?
unit-6-efficient-inefficient-outcomes: Why can a used car that runs perfectly be hard to sell for what it is worth?
Why does a factory that pays all its own bills still produce too much?
When a product harms people nearby who never bought it, why does the market sell too much?
If a vaccine also protects the people around you, why might too few people get one?
How can a government put a price on cleaner air before deciding whether to build a road?
unit-6-efficient-inefficient-outcomes-pa: Should a government tax pollution, ban it, or let firms buy and sell the right to pollute?
If everyone gains from a lighthouse, why might no one choose to pay for it?
Why do fishers who all want fish next year still empty the sea this year?
When should a government stop big firms from merging, fixing prices or growing too powerful?
unit-6-inequality: How can you sum up who gets what in a whole country with a single number?
If almost everyone in a country gets richer, can more people end up counted as poor?
If two workers are equally productive, how can one still end up paid less?
